Highest-value handbook distinction: Three lines of defense
The Study Guide explicitly identifies these responsibilities:
The Study Guide also notes that first- and second-line responsibilities may vary by organizational structure and local regulatory guidance.
Memorize the RCSA steps from Study Guide page 42:
The guide describes RCSA as a collaborative process involving business practitioners, team leaders and fraud experts.

The assurance-review sections deserve special attention. Page 102 discusses a multidisciplinary review team, assessment of fraud indicators, emerging risks, regulatory developments, complaints and grading of program categories. The second line participates in monitoring and testing, while the third line performs independent audit.

A useful distinction for objectives 1.29–1.30 is that payment recall, reversal, chargeback and reimbursement are not interchangeable processes. Study the mechanisms and the jurisdiction-specific conditions separately.

title: Chapter 2 Handbook Mapping
intro: The mapping uses two sources distinctly:
highlights: CAFS Examination Handbook: The 20 examination objectives you supplied.
CAFS Study Guide, Chapter 2: The learning material, examples, case studies and explanations used to satisfy those objectives.

All page references are from the printed Chapter 2 Study Guide, which starts its own numbering at page 1. The uploaded text extract does not itself preserve page boundaries, so I cross-checked the page numbers against the Chapter 2 table of contents in your original ACAMS Study Guide document.
For these five objectives, understand three concepts particularly well:
1. Expected versus suspicious behavior. A fraud detection system needs to recognize normal customer behavior before reliably identifying suspicious deviations.
2. Trend analysis versus data mining. Trend analysis focuses on transaction patterns over time; data mining identifies broader relationships, anomalies and patterns across large datasets.

3. Fraud prevention versus customer experience. Automatically blocking all unusual transactions can increase false positives. Risk-sensitive rules and additional authentication can provide a better balance.

The Study Guide's opening case demonstrates this: an online retailer detects repeated account takeovers involving unusual login devices, changed contact details and unusual transaction patterns. Its preferred response is to build rules-based controls using the identified patterns, rather than block every transaction from a new device.
One particularly important example is a payment immediately following a password reset. The Study Guide identifies this as a higher-risk combination that warrants closer scrutiny.

The Study Guide also distinguishes data mining from data matching. Data mining identifies patterns and relationships; data matching compares and links data points from different sources to uncover inconsistencies and connections.
